oneLineDefinition: A field that builds systems capable of performing tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as recognizing images, understanding language, and making decisions.
overview: AI focuses on creating algorithms and models that allow machines to learn from data and make predictions or decisions. Students study mathematics (linear algebra, calculus, probability), programming, and core ML/DL frameworks. It is more research-oriented and mathematically intensive than Software Engineering or general IT. Graduates can work in both applied engineering and research roles.
typicalProjects: Train an image classifier on a custom dataset
Build a text sentiment analysis model
Fine-tune a pre-trained LLM for a specific task
Build a real-time object detection system
requiredSkills: Strong mathematical reasoning (not just formula memorization)
Ability to read and implement papers in English
Debugging statistical models (not just code bugs)
Patience with iterative experimentation and failed runs
suitableFor: Students who genuinely enjoy applied mathematics and statistics
People who are curious about how systems 'learn' from data
Those who can tolerate ambiguity — models often fail before they work
People comfortable reading dense English-language documentation and papers
Those interested in research or building cutting-edge products
notSuitableFor: Students who want to avoid math beyond basic calculus
Those who expect quick, tangible results — AI projects require many iterations
Students who dislike reading English research papers
Those who only want to build web/mobile apps (Software Engineering is better suited)
keyTakeaways: AI is fundamentally applied mathematics — you cannot avoid it
Most real AI work is 80% data preparation, 20% modeling
English proficiency is non-negotiable — nearly all top resources are in English
The field evolves fast; self-learning ability matters more than memorizing current tools
cautionNotes: Many programs branded 'AI' are actually Software Engineering with a few ML electives — check the curriculum carefully
Knowing how to use ChatGPT or call an API is not the same as studying AI
Starting salaries can be lower than Software Engineering; senior AI roles pay significantly more
marketDemand: High and growing, especially for engineers who can deploy and maintain models in production. Pure research roles are more competitive and typically require graduate degrees.
salaryOutlook: Entry-level AI engineers in Vietnam earn 15-25M VND/month at product companies. Above average among technology majors; strongly dependent on practical experience, specialization, and company type
futureTrend: Demand is shifting from model training to model application and optimization (RAG, fine-tuning, agents). Engineers who can bridge research and production will have strong long-term prospects.
commonMisconceptions: You need a PhD to work in AI — most industry roles require a bachelor's degree with strong practical skills
AI will replace all programmers — in reality, AI increases demand for engineers who can work alongside AI tools
Studying AI means you will build products like ChatGPT — most graduates work on narrower applied problems

faq.question: Does studying AI require very strong math?
faq.answer: Yes. Linear algebra, calculus, and probability are core — not elective. Students who struggle with these subjects will find the program very difficult.

faq.question: Is AI the same as Data Science?
faq.answer: They overlap significantly. Data Science focuses more on data analysis, statistics, and business insight. AI/ML focuses more on building and training predictive models. Many job titles mix both.

faq.question: Can I work in AI if I am not good at coding?
faq.answer: Coding is essential — primarily Python. However, AI roles require less software architecture knowledge than Software Engineering roles. The harder requirement is mathematical fluency.
